headline: Already pushing cyber sales early, illustrating the double-edged sword of pre-emptive discounting in a weak consumer environment
reasoning: Jason Ireland cites JB Hi-Fi as an example of retailers already resorting to early promotional activity (cyber sales) in an attempt to stimulate spending. He frames this as a double-edged sword: while discounting may draw in some traffic, it signals that the normal pre-sale period will generate little revenue as consumers hold back in anticipation of better deals and amid macro uncertainty.
quote: I know JB Hi-Fi is already talking about the cyber sales, and that's the sort of double edged sword, because there's no doubt over the last few years people have saved up a little bit. I think that'll happen even more so this year. So there might be very little other than discounting that you can do leading up to the discount period to get people to spend.
episode_title: Weak confidence puts retailers under pressure

headline: Retailers face a very tough period ahead with little option beyond discounting to drive traffic; consumers likely to hold back spending until uncertainty clears
reasoning: Jason Ireland argues that consumers are saving up and are unlikely to spend freely even if an expected rate hike is avoided, as they anticipate further hikes within months. Discounting is likely the only lever retailers have to drive traffic, as exemplified by JB Hi-Fi already promoting cyber sales ahead of the usual season. Wage growth, while previously supporting spending, is now feeding into an inflation-wage spiral, and employees are becoming uneasy about job security, meaning fewer consumers will feel comfortable spending into the key end-of-year retail period. The advice to retailers is to stay connected with consumers as retail therapy remains a desire, but conditions will be increasingly difficult.
quote: I think what's very interesting now is you've already got some retailers. I know JB Hi-Fi is already talking about the cyber sales, and that's the sort of double edged sword, because there's no doubt over the last few years people have saved up a little bit. I think that'll happen even more so this year. So there might be very little other than discounting that you can do leading up to the discount period to get people to spend, because we're in such an uncertain time, people, if interest rates don't go up in the next couple of weeks, I think many people would think, well, I've dodged that, but probably only for a month or two. So I'm not going to go out and spend like there's no tomorrow. So I think we've got a real period of tough conditions for retailers.
episode_title: Weak confidence puts retailers under pressure

headline: Consumer sentiment has given back all August gains, with fuel costs, interest rates, and housing downturn creating worst retail conditions in ten years
reasoning: Jason Ireland notes the Westpac Melbourne Institute survey showed sentiment falling back towards deeply pessimistic levels, giving back all August gains. Key drivers are fuel prices (seen as uncontrollable by consumers), rising interest rates despite consumers feeling less wealthy, and a housing downturn eroding the wealth effect that had previously supported resilience. He notes that two-thirds of surveyed Australians expect another rate increase, a share that has been gradually growing, and that conditions for retailers are the worst seen in approximately ten years. The combination of housing price declines and rising interest rates is expected to rock discretionary spending even among previously resilient homeowners.
quote: There's no doubt the consumer feels like they're being hit a number of places. Fuel prices are completely out of their control, and for many of them, completely just a fact of their weekly budget. So if fuel price goes up, they can't choose to drive any less or use any less. So it's just a straight hit to their back pocket. I mean, pre during whatever Covid I feel like right now are the worst conditions for retailers that we've seen in the last ten years.
episode_title: Weak confidence puts retailers under pressure

headline: Expecting a prolonged lull in consumer spending as shoppers hold out for cyber and Christmas sales, while retailers face margin compression from wages, utilities, insurance and an inability to raise prices
reasoning: Jason Ireland argues Australian retailers face a particularly difficult period because consumers are deferring discretionary spending in anticipation of major sale events (Black Friday/Cyber Monday in November and post-Christmas). Even if interest rates don't rise imminently, consumers believe relief is only temporary and are unlikely to spend freely. Retailers are simultaneously squeezed on the cost side by wages, fuel, utilities and insurance, and on the revenue side by the need to discount deeply to attract traffic. The expectation for high-quality in-store and online experiences despite shrinking margins makes the environment structurally tough.
quote: I think we've got a real period of tough conditions for retailers. I feel like a broken record. We spoke about this last month. You've got to try and stay connected with your consumer. People like spending money. Retail therapy's a thing. It's just going to be harder and harder. And so you've got to stay connected, try and give that consumer what they want. But it's going to be really tough when consumers know not too far around the corner, some serious sales are going to happen more so this year where they know that retailers are actually struggling. So they're probably going to need to really rely even more on those sales, so we could see a real lull in spending for the next few months... The fact that they can't increase prices, they're going to need to decrease them to get people to come out. And they're also susceptible to our interest rate rises. They are susceptible to fuel rises, wages, utilities, insurance. They're getting crunched at the margin level. And by the way, we all expect the stores to feel great, the experience online to be great. So we all expect more from a retailer with shrinking margin. It's a tough, tough market.
episode_title: Weak confidence puts retailers under pressure

episode_title: Retailers to face a long, cold Christmas?

headline: Jason Ireland sees Australian consumer sentiment remaining deeply depressed with rate cuts the only credible catalyst for a sustained retail recovery.
reasoning: Ireland argues that the consumer remains fundamentally pessimistic despite a small monthly uptick in sentiment, with the improvement primarily driven by relief that rates did not rise rather than optimism about the future. He sees the risk skewed to rates staying higher for longer or even rising, which will continue to suppress discretionary spending. The only genuine catalyst for improvement would be rate cuts or credible forward guidance on cuts, which may be a long way off given global macro uncertainties.
quote: I think that's really it. And as your previous guest talked to a little bit, there's still some factors going on in the global economy that say that that could be a way off yet. So we're just in this for the for the foreseeable future I think. Interestingly, the majority of the uptick in this month was from mortgage holders happy with the result of it not going up. So you can see how much underlying concern there is that it's up rather than down from here.
episode_title: Retailers to face a long, cold Christmas?

headline: McGrathNicol's Jason Ireland sees sustained 12-month period of difficulty for Australian discretionary retailers as consumer sentiment remains deeply pessimistic and cost pressures mount.
reasoning: Ireland notes that while consumer sentiment has ticked up slightly, it remains deeply pessimistic, with the family finances sub-index still only at 80. Retailers face a double squeeze: they cannot raise prices (in fact must discount to drive traffic) while their fixed cost base is rising. He expects retailers will bring sales forward to convert inventory into cash, but sees a tough 12-month period ahead. The key catalyst for improvement would be rate cuts or credible chatter about rate cuts, which he suggests may still be a long way off given global economic uncertainty.
quote: I think we're going to see a really sustained period of of discretionary spending being being very tight. There's no doubt. And I think you've seen many of the retailers who are coming out now. JB Hi-Fi are Myer a while back their executive chair talking about looking forward. It's flat maybe even at best with margin pressure. The things we've been talking about is you've got no ability to raise prices. In fact, you've got a discount to get people through the door. Yet your underlying cost of doing business is going up. So I think we've got two things happening with retailers. We've got a difficulty in stimulating revenue and cost base, fixed cost base as well. Going up, I think it just points to the fact that we're probably going to see sales earlier to try and stimulate and turn this stock that people are buying now into cash, because I think we're going to see a sort of period of 12 months of, of difficulties.
episode_title: Retailers to face a long, cold Christmas?
